# From data to a genomic figure

Genomic figures often combine exon positions on a chromosome, links between
genomes, signal depth, and positions along a protein. ggexon connects these
views through stored annotations and a ggplot2 plotting grammar.

Each example below presents the input, constructs or prepares the ggexon
object, and chooses geoms, scales, and a theme. The small gene models,
gene-order matrix, protein counts, and DNA strings are synthetic teaching
data. The pairwise and coverage examples use bundled files. Run the chunks
in order in an R session with the current version of ggexon installed.

```{r libraries, warning = FALSE}
library(ggexon)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Major data objects

| Object | What it stores | Typical input |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SynFeatureAnnotation` | Genes, transcripts, exons, and CDS | GFF3 or GTF |
| `SynIndividual` | One genome or sample and its annotation layers | Annotation, optional FASTA |
| `SynSpecies` | Individuals and comparative relationships | Individuals, alignments, homology, trees |
| `SynPairAlignment`, `SynMultiAlignment` | Relationships between genomes | PAF/PSL, or supported multiple-alignment data |
| `SynBigWigAnnotation`, `SynVCFAnnotation` | Region-queryable signal or variants | BigWig or VCF |
| `SynProteinDomainAnnotation`, `SynProteinMutationAnnotation` | Domains or mutation summaries | Domain and mutation tables |
| `SynAnnotationPatch` | An explicit gene-model correction | Corrected feature ranges |
| `HomologyAnnotation` | Reference/query gene mappings | Curated table or imported BLAST results |
| `SynLayout`, `SynLocusSet` | Reusable panel windows or comparable loci | Named coordinate windows |

## Plotting functions supplied by ggexon

`ggexon()` starts the figure. Syn-aware layers resolve stored annotations
when the plot is built; table-based layers use prepared data. Ordinary
ggplot2 scales and themes remain available. A theme changes appearance; it
does not select a genomic window or transform coordinates.

### Geoms

| Function | What it draws |
| --- | --- |
| `geom_exon()` | Exon rectangles, transcript backbones, and strand direction |
| `geom_exon2()` | Exon/CDS/UTR models with explicit introns and optional schematic compression |
| `geom_genetag()` | One directional gene span, with optional labels and overlap lanes |
| `geom_genebox()` | Equal-size gene boxes with internal strand arrows |
| `geom_genelabel()` | Gene labels and their leader lines, including homology-based names |
| `geom_genelink()` | Straight, elbow, or spline lines between supplied coordinate pairs |
| `geom_nuclink()` | Nucleotide-alignment ribbons between genomic panels |
| `geom_synteny_link()` | Interval ribbons for supplied gene, exon, or block relationships |
| `geom_coverage()` | Continuous coverage or signal tracks |
| `geom_motif()` | Motif/domain blocks; attached protein domains can be projected onto genomic CDS intervals |
| `geom_aa_variant()` | Amino-acid variant markers projected onto transcript models |
| `geom_protein_lollipop()` | A protein backbone, domain blocks, and mutation stems and heads |
| `geom_mutation_label()` | Mutation labels positioned to match mutation markers |
| `geom_alignseq()` | Anchored DNA-difference markers or aligned sequence rows |
| `geom_genomic_tree()` | Attaches a rectangular tree for alignment with genomic panels |

### Scales and guides

| Function | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| `scale_x_ggexon_genomic()` | Shared exon-aware intron compression with original genomic coordinate labels |
| `guide_x_ggexon_piecewise()` | Representative exon and intron scale bars for the compressed genomic x scale |
| `strip_scale_x()` | Gene-order display widths or explicit shared comparison slots |
| `strip_scale()` | Compatibility alias for `strip_scale_x()` |
| `scale_x_facet_labels()` | Different x-axis labels for facets sharing a continuous x scale |
| `scale_panel_annotation()` | Shared or independent annotation-panel y scales, with optional visible limits |
| `scale_panel_coverage()` | Shared or independent coverage-panel y scales, with optional manual or automatic visible limits |

### Facets and panel layout

| Function | What it arranges |
| --- | --- |
| `facet_genomics()` | Annotation, coverage, and intervening link panels |
| `facet_genomictree()` | Genomic panels ordered by tree tips, beside one spanning tree |
| `center_panel_annotation()` | Centers annotation bodies in their panel views |
| `set_panel_xlim()`, `clear_panel_xlim()` | Store or clear per-individual genomic windows |
| `effective_panel_windows()` | Inspect the annotation windows resolved for a plot or stored layout |
| `locus_grid_layout()`, `use_locus_grid()` | Prepare and apply layouts for comparable locus windows |
| `annotate_cross_panel()` | Connect explicitly supplied anchors across panels |
| `link_panels()` | Connect matching IDs represented by anchors in different panels |

### Themes

| Function | When to use it |
| --- | --- |
| `theme_ggexon_base()` | A background-free foundation retaining ordinary axes and grids |
| `theme_ggexon_clean()` | The named shortcut for that clean background-free styling |
| `theme_ggexon_track()` | Compact genomic tracks, with control over axes, grids, and legends |
| `theme_ggexon_pairwise()` | Stacked annotation/link/annotation comparisons |
| `theme_ggexon_genomictree()` | Genomic tracks aligned beside a tree |
| `theme_ggexon_side_strips()` | Horizontal facet labels on the left or right, added after a complete theme |

### Plot preparation and output

| Function | What it prepares |
| --- | --- |
| `alignseq_data()` | Anchored columns and difference events from two already aligned DNA strings |
| `protein_lollipop_data()` | Protein backbone, domain, and mutation layout tables |
| `protein_mutation_data()` | Access the normalized table in a protein-mutation annotation |
| `syn_gr_to_exon_df()` | Convert genomic feature ranges to an exon plotting table |
| `project_domains_to_genome()`, `project_mutations_to_genome()` | Map protein positions through transcript CDS blocks to genomic intervals |
| `ggexon_output_size()` | Record the intended figure dimensions for downstream layout |

Functions such as `aes()`, `scale_fill_manual()`, `scale_x_continuous()`,
`facet_wrap()`, `coord_fixed()`, `theme()`, and `ggsave()` come from ggplot2.
The examples combine these with the ggexon functions above.

# 1. Exons and alternative transcripts

An exon table contains intervals and transcript membership. Drawing each row
as an unrelated rectangle loses introns and strand direction. `geom_exon()`
uses the feature hierarchy to draw transcript models.

## Present the input

Create two synthetic genes on `chr1`. Gene A has a full transcript and an
exon-skipping transcript; gene B is on the opposite strand. Coordinates are
one-based and inclusive, as in GTF. These are teaching models, not observed
gene annotations.

```{r workflow-feature-input}
features <- data.frame(
  type = c("gene", "transcript", rep("exon", 3), rep("CDS", 3),
           "transcript", rep("exon", 2), rep("CDS", 2),
           "gene", "transcript", "exon", "exon"),
  start = c(101, 101, 101, 501, 901, 101, 501, 901,
            101, 101, 901, 101, 901, 1201, 1201, 1201, 1501),
  end = c(960, 960, 160, 590, 960, 160, 590, 960,
          960, 160, 960, 160, 960, 1560, 1560, 1260, 1560),
  strand = c(rep("+", 13), rep("-", 4)),
  gene_id = c(rep("geneA", 13), rep("geneB", 4)),
  transcript_id = c(NA, rep("A_full", 7), rep("A_skip", 5),
                    NA, rep("B_only", 3))
)
knitr::kable(features)
```

Write the records as a standard nine-column GTF. Substitute your own GTF or
GFF3 path when working with real annotations.

```{r workflow-write-gtf}
attributes <- paste0('gene_id "', features$gene_id, '";')
has_transcript <- !is.na(features$transcript_id)
attributes[has_transcript] <- paste0(
  attributes[has_transcript], ' transcript_id "',
  features$transcript_id[has_transcript], '";'
)
gtf <- data.frame(
  seqname = "chr1", source = "synthetic", type = features$type,
  start = features$start, end = features$end, score = ".",
  strand = features$strand,
  phase = ifelse(features$type == "CDS", "0", "."), attributes = attributes
)
gtf_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".gtf")
write.table(gtf, gtf_file, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE,
            row.names = FALSE, col.names = FALSE)
```

## Construct and inspect the object

`SynIndividual(annotation_file = ...)` attaches a default
`SynFeatureAnnotation`. A FASTA is optional for annotation plotting; sequence
extraction and translation require one. `load_annotation()` materializes the
features so that we can inspect them before drawing.

```{r workflow-feature-object}
model <- SynIndividual(
  annotation_file = gtf_file, annotation_format = "gtf", id = "teaching"
)
model <- load_annotation(model)
class(model)
class(get_annotation(model))
exons <- query_features(model, feature_type = "exon", all = TRUE)
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(exons)[,
  c("seqnames", "start", "end", "strand", "gene_id", "transcript_id")])
```

## Choose the geom, scales, and theme

Map transcript IDs to fill to distinguish isoforms. The ordinary continuous
x scale preserves genomic spacing. The track theme hides the y axis used to
position models; `show_legend = TRUE` retains the transcript legend.

```{r workflow-exons, fig.alt = "Synthetic exon models: A full has three exons, A skip omits the middle exon, and B only is on the minus strand."}
transcript_colours <- c(A_full = "#0072B2", A_skip = "#D55E00", B_only = "#009E73")
p_exons <- ggexon(model) +
  geom_exon(
    aes(fill = transcript_id), chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 1600),
    transcript_arrow_length = 30
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = transcript_colours, name = "Transcript") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(100, 500, 900, 1300, 1600),
                     labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_legend = TRUE)
p_exons
```

The x distances are base pairs. The missing middle exon in `A_skip` comes
from the input annotation; ggexon does not infer alternative splicing.

# 2. Compress introns while retaining genomic labels

Long introns can make exons too small to compare. A shared exon-aware scale
compresses gaps while keeping transcripts aligned, helping you compare exon
structure across isoforms.

## Present the input

Reuse the synthetic GTF and inspect gene A's exon rows.

```{r workflow-compression-input}
knitr::kable(features[features$gene_id == "geneA" & features$type == "exon", ])
```

## Prepare the object

Create a copy restricted to the first locus, leaving `model` reusable.

```{r workflow-compression-object}
gene_a <- subset_individual(model, chr = "chr1", start = 80, end = 980)
query_features(gene_a, feature_type = "exon", all = TRUE)
```

## Choose the geom, scales, and theme

`geom_exon2()` draws explicit chevron introns. Disable its schematic
compression so `scale_x_ggexon_genomic()` controls the transformation across
the panel. A factor of 8 displays eligible gaps at one eighth of their
genomic length while preserving exon widths.

```{r workflow-compressed-exons, fig.alt = "Two gene A transcripts with chevron introns compressed eightfold and original genomic tick labels."}
p_compressed <- ggexon(gene_a) +
  geom_exon2(
    aes(fill = transcript_id), chr = "chr1", compress_introns = FALSE,
    arrow_width = 12
  ) +
  scale_x_ggexon_genomic(intron_factor = 8, n.breaks = 4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = transcript_colours, name = "Transcript") +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_legend = TRUE)
p_compressed
```

Ticks report original genomic positions, but equal display distances across
exons and introns no longer imply equal base-pair distances. A piecewise
guide can show separate representative exon and intron scale bars.

```{r workflow-piecewise-guide, fig.alt = "The compressed gene A models with representative exon and intron scale bars."}
ggexon(gene_a) +
  geom_exon2(
    aes(fill = transcript_id), chr = "chr1", compress_introns = FALSE,
    arrow_width = 12
  ) +
  scale_x_ggexon_genomic(
    intron_factor = 8, guide = guide_x_ggexon_piecewise(by = "panel")
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = transcript_colours) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10)
```

With explicit CDS and UTR records, `geom_exon2(annotation_type = "all")`
can distinguish their box heights. Its default `compress_introns = TRUE`
offers another schematic view; choose one compression method deliberately.

# 3. Gene spans and readable labels

For a locus overview, transcript detail can hide gene order. A directional
tag gives one span per gene. Separate labels keep names readable without
replacing the stable gene IDs used in computation.

## Present the input

```{r workflow-tag-input}
knitr::kable(features[features$type == "gene",
                      c("gene_id", "start", "end", "strand")])
labels <- c(geneA = "Gene A (two isoforms)", geneB = "Gene B")
```

## Prepare the object

`set_gene_labels()` returns an updated object carrying plot labels alongside
the original IDs.

```{r workflow-tag-object}
labelled_model <- set_gene_labels(model, labels)
```

## Choose the geom, scales, and theme

Suppress built-in tag labels and add `geom_genelabel()` for explicit
placement. `collapse_tandem = TRUE` also combines adjacent genes sharing a
label. Retain a base-pair axis because gene spans and spacing matter here.

```{r workflow-genetags, fig.height = 2.8, fig.alt = "Directional gene spans with readable labels above the synthetic locus."}
ggexon(labelled_model) +
  geom_genetag(aes(fill = gene_id), chr = "chr1", show_label = FALSE) +
  geom_genelabel(chr = "chr1", label_direction = "top", size = 3,
                 collapse_tandem = TRUE, panel_width_inch = 7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(geneA = "#0072B2", geneB = "#009E73")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ","),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0.08)) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10)
```

For crowded loci, `gene_layout = "stack"` or `"nested"` separates overlapping
bodies. For cross-species names, attach a `HomologyAnnotation` to a
`SynSpecies` and use it through `geom_genelabel()`. Labels alone do not
establish homology.

# 4. Pairwise nucleotide alignments

Two genomes can contain the same locus at different chromosome positions.
`SynSpecies` stores their annotations and alignment together;
`facet_genomics()` places links between their source tracks.

## Present the input

Use the bundled XZ1516 and N2 annotations and a small PAF alignment. This
example needs neither a download nor user-supplied files.

```{r workflow-pairwise-input}
compact_dir <- system.file("extdata", "compact_synspecies", package = "ggexon")
xz_gff <- file.path(compact_dir, "caenorhabditis_XZ1516.gff3")
n2_gtf <- file.path(compact_dir, "c_elegans.PRJNA13758.WS285.canonical_geneset.gtf")
paf_file <- file.path(compact_dir, "V_alginment.paf")
stopifnot(file.exists(xz_gff), file.exists(n2_gtf), file.exists(paf_file))
cat(readLines(xz_gff, n = 5), sep = "\n")
cat(readLines(n2_gtf, n = 3), sep = "\n")
raw_paf <- read.delim(paf_file, header = FALSE, comment.char = "")
names(raw_paf)[1:12] <- c(
  "query", "qlen", "qstart", "qend", "strand", "target", "tlen",
  "tstart", "tend", "matches", "alen", "mapq"
)
knitr::kable(head(raw_paf[, c("query", "qstart", "qend", "strand", "alen")], 4))
knitr::kable(head(raw_paf[, c("target", "tstart", "tend", "matches", "mapq")], 4))
```

Raw PAF uses zero-based starts and half-open intervals. The ggexon importer
normalizes returned start/end columns to one-based closed intervals. Let it
perform this conversion once.

## Construct and inspect the objects

```{r workflow-pairwise-object}
xz <- SynIndividual(annotation_file = xz_gff, id = "XZ1516")
n2 <- SynIndividual(annotation_file = n2_gtf, annotation_format = "gtf", id = "N2")
comparison <- SynSpecies(name = "Caenorhabditis pair")
comparison <- add_individual(comparison, xz)
comparison <- add_individual(comparison, n2)
comparison <- add_pairwise_alignment(
  comparison,
  SynPairAlignment(
    name = "XZ1516_vs_N2", query_individual = "XZ1516",
    target_individual = "N2", file = paf_file, format = "paf"
  )
)
individual_names(comparison)
aligned_blocks <- pairwise_alignment_data(
  comparison, alignment = "XZ1516_vs_N2",
  subset = c(XZ1516 = "RagTag_V:21574445-21584356"), filter = 200
)
knitr::kable(head(aligned_blocks[, intersect(
  c("qname", "qstart", "qend", "tname", "tstart", "tend", "strand", "alen"),
  names(aligned_blocks)
)], 6))
```

`filter = 200` removes short alignment fragments from this query result,
leaving the stored alignment unchanged. `subset_pairwise_alignment()` and
`filter_pairwise_alignment()` expose these operations separately.

## Choose the geom, scales, facet, and theme

`geom_nuclink()` derives a comparison window from XZ1516 coordinates and
resolves the corresponding N2 region. Independent x ranges show each
genome's own positions. The annotation y policy controls model layout. Hide the link panel's axes
because the ribbons connect the two annotation rulers rather than defining
a third genomic coordinate system.

```{r workflow-pairwise-plot, fig.height = 4.4, fig.alt = "N2 and XZ1516 exon models connected by nucleotide alignment ribbons."}
p_pairwise <- ggexon(comparison) +
  geom_exon(species = c("N2", "XZ1516"), fill = "#0072B2") +
  geom_nuclink(
    reference = "XZ1516", chr = "RagTag_V",
    subset = c(21574445, 21584356), alignment = "XZ1516_vs_N2",
    fill = "#56B4E9", alpha = 0.55
  ) +
  facet_genomics(vars(track), scales = "free_x", ncol = 1,
                 strip.position = "left", vertical = "center",
                 link_axis = "none", link_strip = "blank", link_panel_height = 0.6) +
  scale_panel_annotation("fixed_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  theme_ggexon_pairwise(base_size = 10)
p_pairwise
```

The GFF uses `V_RagTag`; the resolver also accepts the `RagTag_V` alias used
in the plotting call. Inspect seqnames when preparing your own files.

Omitting `species` on a `SynSpecies` exon layer selects all stored
individuals. Select it explicitly for a subset. For repeated figures,
`set_panel_xlim()` stores named per-individual windows on the comparison's
`SynLayout`; `clear_panel_xlim()` removes the overrides.

`SynMultiAlignment` supports ODGI-backed comparisons. It can store already
parsed MAF data through `data`, but `load_alignment()` does not parse MAF
files. The [class and verb reference](ggexon-classes-and-verbs.html)
describes these larger workflows.

# 5. Gene-level synteny from an interval table

A curated ortholog link has a different interpretation from a nucleotide
alignment. `geom_synteny_link()` draws supplied interval relationships with
the same panel machinery; it does not infer those relationships.

## Present the input

Two synthetic loci contain matched genes at different positions. The
`family` assignments are supplied teaching data.

```{r workflow-synteny-input}
panel_order <- c("reference", "link_reference_query", "query")
genes <- data.frame(
  track = factor(rep(c("reference", "query"), each = 2), levels = panel_order),
  xmin = c(100, 400, 1100, 1600), xmax = c(250, 600, 1300, 1750),
  y = 1, strand = c("+", "-", "+", "-"), gene = rep(c("A", "B"), 2)
)
relationships <- data.frame(
  family = c("A", "B"), tstart = c(100, 400), tend = c(250, 600),
  qstart = c(1100, 1600), qend = c(1300, 1750), strand = "+"
)
knitr::kable(genes)
knitr::kable(relationships)
```

## Prepare the plotting data

Tables are valid inputs too. Add source track and chromosome names to route
ribbons to their annotation panels. This prepared table workflow does not
require a `SynPairAlignment`.

```{r workflow-synteny-object}
synteny <- transform(
  relationships,
  track = factor("link_reference_query", levels = panel_order),
  tspecies = "reference", tchr = "chr1",
  qspecies = "query", qchr = "chr2", group = seq_len(nrow(relationships))
)
```

## Choose the geom, scales, facet, and theme

Share a named palette between tags and ribbons so colour has one meaning.
Independent base-pair axes retain the two loci's native coordinates.

```{r workflow-synteny-plot, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "Synthetic gene pairs connected by ribbons coloured by supplied family assignments."}
ggexon() +
  geom_genetag(data = genes, aes(fill = gene), show_label = FALSE) +
  geom_synteny_link(
    data = synteny,
    aes(tspecies = tspecies, tchr = tchr, tstart = tstart, tend = tend,
        qspecies = qspecies, qchr = qchr, qstart = qstart, qend = qend,
        strand = strand, group = group, fill = family),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.45
  ) +
  facet_genomics(vars(track), scales = "free_x", ncol = 1,
                 strip.position = "left", vertical = "center",
                 link_axis = "none", link_strip = "blank", link_panel_height = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(A = "#0072B2", B = "#D55E00"), name = "Family") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_number()) +
  theme_ggexon_pairwise(base_size = 10, show_legend = TRUE)
```

# 6. Raw BigWig coverage beside gene annotation

Comparing a continuous signal with a gene model requires a shared genomic
window and a separate quantitative y scale. Signal layers keep the raw
measurements attached to the individual rather than mixing them into feature
annotation rows.

## Present the input

The bundled PEEL-1 fixture contains raw depth BigWigs and a WS285 GTF subset.
Here two strains share one chromosome-I window. Start by inspecting the GTF
as text: its nine columns contain genomic coordinates and feature attributes.
BigWig is binary, so inspect its records with a region query instead of a text
reader. The BigWig backend runs on macOS and Linux, and is unsupported on Windows.

```{r workflow-coverage-input, eval = .Platform$OS.type != "windows"}
coverage_dir <- system.file("extdata", "peel1_coverage", package = "ggexon")
coverage_gtf <- file.path(coverage_dir, "WS285.ugt31-zeel1-peel1-nekl1.gtf")
coverage_strains <- c("XZ1516", "ECA2091")
cat(readLines(coverage_gtf, n = 5), sep = "\n")

first_signal <- SynBigWigAnnotation(
  name = "coverage",
  bigwig_file = file.path(coverage_dir, "XZ1516.raw.bw"),
  metadata = list(signal_unit = "raw_depth")
)
head(as.data.frame(query_signal(
  first_signal, chr = "I", start = 2332338L, end = 2373985L
)))
```

`query_signal()` returns intervals with a `score`, rather than requiring one
row for every base. The imported table uses 1-based inclusive genomic
coordinates. The metadata records the unit; it does not normalize the scores.

## Construct and inspect the objects

```{r workflow-coverage-object, eval = .Platform$OS.type != "windows"}
coverage_species <- SynSpecies(name = "PEEL-1 coverage")
for (strain in coverage_strains) {
  one_strain <- SynIndividual(
    annotation_file = coverage_gtf, annotation_format = "gtf", id = strain
  )
  one_strain <- add_annotation(one_strain, SynBigWigAnnotation(
    name = "coverage",
    bigwig_file = file.path(coverage_dir, paste0(strain, ".raw.bw")),
    metadata = list(signal_unit = "raw_depth")
  ))
  coverage_species <- add_individual(coverage_species, one_strain)
}
individual_names(coverage_species)
```

Each individual owns a gene model and a named signal layer. `geom_coverage()`
resolves that layer for both strains; the exon request supplies their common
viewing window and draws one representative gene model below the signals.

## Choose the geom, scales, facet, and theme

```{r workflow-coverage-plot, eval = .Platform$OS.type != "windows", fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Raw coverage from two C. elegans strains above a shared four-gene annotation, with one shared depth scale."}
coverage_layers <- ggexon(coverage_species) +
  geom_coverage(annotation = "coverage", fill = "#4C78A8") +
  geom_exon(
    species = "XZ1516", chr = "I", subset = c(2332338L, 2373985L),
    annotation_type = "exon"
  ) +
  facet_genomics(vars(track), ncol = 1, strip.position = "left") +
  center_panel_annotation() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), oob = scales::oob_keep) +
  labs(x = "Chromosome I position (bp)") +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10) +
  theme_ggexon_side_strips("left", base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_text())
coverage_plot <- coverage_layers + scale_panel_coverage("fixed_y")
coverage_plot
```

The explicit `fixed_y` policy makes equal vertical heights comparable across
coverage panels. `center_panel_annotation()` adjusts the separate annotation
panel's view. The track theme hides y labels used for annotation layout, while
the side strip helper turns strain labels into readable horizontal text.
This view compares signal shape and shared heights; inspect the queried
`score` values for exact depths because y tick labels are hidden.
The large ECA2091 peak sets the shared depth range, making the other signal
look low. `oob_keep` retains boundary intervals for clipping at the panel edge.

Replace the coverage policy with `scale_panel_coverage("free_y")` to inspect
each strain on its own depth range; equal heights then need not mean equal
depth. Adding `auto = TRUE` places each panel's span-weighted median at 85%
of its height and clips higher peaks in the view. Neither option changes raw
scores. Keep a linear genomic x axis: exon/intron compression through
`scale_x_ggexon_genomic()` is unsupported for continuous coverage tracks.

```{r workflow-coverage-free, eval = .Platform$OS.type != "windows", fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "The same raw coverage signals on separate y ranges, with each median depth at 85 percent of panel height and higher peaks clipped."}
coverage_layers + scale_panel_coverage("free_y", auto = TRUE)
```

This second view reveals local signal structure in each strain. The peak
clipping and independent y ranges mean its panel heights cannot be compared
as absolute depths. See the [coverage example](bigwig-coverage-demo.html)
for the full strain panel and fixture provenance.

# 7. Protein mutation counts and domains

A protein summary removes introns from the view and places mutation counts
next to functional regions. This helps compare residues across a protein
without treating their genomic distances as protein distances.

## Present the input

Protein positions and genomic positions describe different coordinate systems.
For this example, create a synthetic mutation summary for a 160-residue
protein, plus two synthetic domain intervals. These are teaching data, not
biological claims. Counts describe samples carrying each mutation.

```{r workflow-protein-input}
raw_mutations <- data.frame(
  gene = "demo-protein",
  event_type = "substitution",
  mutation_hash_or_notation = c("A#18#V", "K#42#R", "G#88#D", "S#140#F"),
  sample_count = c(2L, 5L, 12L, 20L)
)
protein_domains <- data.frame(
  start = c(10L, 85L), end = c(60L, 145L),
  Domain = c("Binding", "Catalytic")
)
raw_mutations
protein_domains
```

The reader bridges a raw count file and the normalized mutation table expected
by the annotation object. It adds `gene_id`, `position`, `ref`, `alt`,
`mutation`, and `source_row_id`. Passing `mutation_data` to the constructor
stores this already normalized table; the constructor does not parse it again.

## Construct and inspect the object

```{r workflow-protein-object}
mutation_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".tsv")
write.table(raw_mutations, mutation_file, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)
normalized_mutations <- read_protein_mutation_counts(mutation_file)
protein_individual <- add_annotation(
  SynIndividual(id = "synthetic-cohort"),
  SynProteinMutationAnnotation(
    name = "mutation_counts", mutation_file = mutation_file,
    mutation_data = normalized_mutations
  )
)
protein_mutations <- query_protein_mutations(
  protein_individual, annotation = "mutation_counts", genes = "demo-protein"
)
protein_mutations[, c("gene_id", "position", "ref", "alt", "mutation", "sample_count")]
```

`geom_protein_lollipop()` takes ordinary mutation and domain tables, so query
the attached annotation first. Inspect its preparation helper to see how
positions become backbone, domain, stem, and head data. With the identity
transform and the target range equal to the observed count range, the helper
keeps head heights equal to sample counts for these data.

## Choose the geom, scales, and theme

```{r workflow-protein-preparation}
count_range <- range(protein_mutations$sample_count)
prepared_protein <- protein_lollipop_data(
  mutations = protein_mutations, domains = protein_domains, protein_length = 160,
  mutation_y_by = "sample_count", mutation_y_range = count_range,
  track_ymin = -1.5, track_ymax = -1,
  domain_default_ymin = -1.8, domain_default_ymax = -0.7
)
prepared_protein$mutations[, c("position", "lollipop_x", "lollipop_y", "lollipop_domain")]
```

```{r workflow-protein-plot, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Synthetic protein domains with four mutation lollipops whose heights show sample counts of two, five, twelve, and twenty."}
protein_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_protein_lollipop(
    mutations = protein_mutations, domains = protein_domains, protein_length = 160,
    mutation_y_by = "sample_count", mutation_y_range = count_range,
    track_ymin = -1.5, track_ymax = -1,
    domain_default_ymin = -1.8, domain_default_ymax = -0.7,
    point_colour = "#222222", point_size = 2.5
  ) +
  geom_mutation_label(
    mutations = protein_mutations, mutation_y_by = "sample_count",
    mutation_y_range = count_range, label_nudge_y = 0.8,
    angle = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Binding = "#0072B2", Catalytic = "#E69F00")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 160, 40), limits = c(0, 160)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20), limits = c(-2, 23)) +
  labs(x = "Amino-acid position", y = "Samples with mutation", fill = "Domain") +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_y_axis = TRUE, show_legend = TRUE) +
  theme(axis.title = element_text())
protein_plot
```

The label layer repeats the head-height settings so each label follows its
mutation. Domain blocks sit below zero; the labeled y ticks refer to sample
counts. Keeping `show_y_axis = TRUE` matters here because y carries a measured
quantity. With the default lollipop height range, heights would be rescaled
layout positions and should not be labeled as raw counts. No genomic x scale
or facet is needed for this single protein-coordinate track.

## Project protein features onto the genomic model

A protein residue number is not a chromosome coordinate. Projection follows
the transcript's CDS blocks, so one protein interval can occupy several exons.
This example reconnects gene A's isoforms with a synthetic genome, then places
a domain and a mutation on the exon models in genomic base pairs.

### Present the raw data

Reuse `gtf_file` from the first example. Its full transcript contains three
CDS blocks; `A_skip` uses the first and last. Fill a 1,700-base `chr1` with
unknown bases, then insert complete coding blocks. The first block starts
with `ATG`, the last ends with `TAA`, and all CDS phases are zero.

```{r workflow-projection-input}
coding_blocks <- data.frame(
  start = c(101L, 501L, 901L), end = c(160L, 590L, 960L),
  dna = c(paste0("ATG", strrep("GCC", 19)), strrep("GCC", 30),
          paste0(strrep("GCC", 19), "TAA"))
)
coding_blocks$width <- nchar(coding_blocks$dna)
knitr::kable(coding_blocks[, c("start", "end", "width")])
domain_input <- data.frame(
  transcript_id = "A_full", domain = "Teaching domain",
  start = 15L, end = 30L, analysis = "Pfam"
)
mutation_input <- data.frame(
  gene_id = "geneA", position = 25L, ref = "A", alt = "V",
  sample_count = 4L, mutation = "A25V", source_row_id = 1L
)
knitr::kable(domain_input)
knitr::kable(mutation_input)
```

Domain bounds and mutation positions above are one-based **amino-acid**
coordinates. The mutation table is already normalized; `source_row_id`
records its input row. It describes one synthetic gene-level mutation,
which will be projected separately onto each matching isoform.

### Construct the sequence and annotation objects

Create a FASTA and a new `SynIndividual` using the existing GTF. Translation
joins each transcript's CDS in coding order. The output below contains 70
characters for `A_full` and 40 for `A_skip`, including a terminal `*`.

```{r workflow-projection-sequence}
sequence_bases <- rep("N", 1700)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(coding_blocks))) {
  positions <- seq.int(coding_blocks$start[i], coding_blocks$end[i])
  sequence_bases[positions] <- strsplit(coding_blocks$dna[i], "")[[1]]
}
teaching_fasta <- tempfile(fileext = ".fa")
writeLines(c(">chr1", paste0(sequence_bases, collapse = "")), teaching_fasta)
sequence_model <- SynIndividual(
  genome_file = teaching_fasta, annotation_file = gtf_file,
  annotation_format = "gtf", id = "teaching-sequence"
)
sequence_model <- translate_protein(sequence_model, genes = "geneA")
translated <- as.character(protein_seq(sequence_model))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  transcript = names(translated), residues_including_stop = nchar(translated),
  sequence_start = substr(unname(translated), 1, 12),
  terminal_character = substr(unname(translated), nchar(translated), nchar(translated))
))
```

Attach domains using an explicit transcript key, and store the normalized
mutation table in memory. The `analysis` column identifies the domain model;
`model = "Pfam"` selects its records during projection.

```{r workflow-projection-annotations}
teaching_domain_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".tsv")
write.table(domain_input, teaching_domain_file, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE,
            row.names = FALSE)
sequence_model <- add_annotation(sequence_model, SynProteinDomainAnnotation(
  name = "teaching_domains", domain_file = teaching_domain_file,
  keytype = "transcript_id"
))
sequence_model <- add_annotation(sequence_model, SynProteinMutationAnnotation(
  name = "teaching_mutations", mutation_file = "<in-memory>",
  keytype = "gene_id", mutation_data = mutation_input, lazy = FALSE
))
domain_projection <- project_domains_to_genome(
  sequence_model, annotation = "teaching_domains", model = "Pfam",
  transcripts = "A_full"
)
mutation_projection <- project_mutations_to_genome(
  sequence_model, annotation = "teaching_mutations", genes = "geneA"
)
knitr::kable(domain_projection[, c("transcripts", "xmin", "xmax", "motif")])
knitr::kable(mutation_projection[, c("transcripts", "xmin", "xmax", "mutation")])
```

The domain splits into genomic intervals 143-160 and 501-530. Residue 25
maps to 513-515 in `A_full` and 913-915 in `A_skip`: identical protein
positions need not refer to identical genomic bases across isoforms.

### Choose the geoms, scale, and theme

Draw neutral exon models, overlay the projected domain on the `A_full` row,
and add mutation lollipops aligned to their matching transcripts. Here
`y_offset = 2` places the single domain row over `A_full` in this two-isoform
layout; inspect row placement when changing transcripts or domain models.

```{r workflow-projection-plot, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Gene A exon models in genomic coordinates, with a split domain on the full isoform and residue 25 mutation markers at different genomic codons in the two isoforms."}
projection_plot <- ggexon(sequence_model) +
  geom_exon(chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 980), fill = "grey85",
            colour = "grey50", transcript_arrow_length = 25) +
  geom_motif(aes(fill = motif), annotation = "teaching_domains", model = "Pfam",
             chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 980), y_offset = 2, exon_height = 0.5) +
  geom_aa_variant(aes(fill = mutation, label = mutation),
    annotation = "teaching_mutations", genes = "geneA",
    chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 980), spread = FALSE,
    colour = "grey20", label_angle = 0, label_size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Teaching domain" = "#0072B2", A25V = "#D55E00"),
                    name = "Protein feature") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(100, 500, 900),
                     labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_legend = TRUE)
projection_plot
```

This x axis measures genomic base pairs. The preceding protein lollipop
example measures amino-acid positions. Projection uses annotation structure;
the plotted mutation is supplied teaching data, not a variant inferred from
the synthetic FASTA.

# 8. Aligned DNA and sequence differences

An alignment ribbon summarizes an interval but hides the bases that differ.
For a short verified pairwise alignment, `alignseq_data()` attaches columns
to genomic positions and `geom_alignseq()` draws the sequence detail.

## Present the input

Supply two already aligned strings. A dash is a gap; each start coordinate
identifies the first non-gap base in the supplied orientation.

```{r workflow-dna-input}
dna <- c(reference = "AC-GTAC", query = "ATCG-AC")
anchors <- data.frame(
  sequence = names(dna), start = c(100, 900), strand = "+",
  track = names(dna), chr = c("chr1", "chr2")
)
knitr::kable(data.frame(sequence = names(dna), aligned_DNA = unname(dna)))
knitr::kable(anchors)
```

## Prepare and inspect the data

The helper returns a data frame rather than an S4 container. It classifies
differences relative to the named reference; it does not compute an alignment
or infer evolutionary direction.

```{r workflow-dna-object}
dna_columns <- alignseq_data(
  aligned = dna, anchors = anchors, reference = "reference",
  details = c(101, 103), flank = 1
)
knitr::kable(dna_columns[, c("track", "column", "base", "position", "event_type")])
```

## Choose the geom, scales, and theme

The row view suits this seven-column alignment. Each panel keeps its own
genomic axis. Base callouts have equal column spacing; gaps consume no
genomic bases. The geom supplies fixed event colours and nucleotide
backgrounds, leaving the plot's fill scale available for other layers.

```{r workflow-dna-plot, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "Two aligned DNA rows anchored to their genomic coordinates, showing a substitution and two gap events."}
ggexon() +
  geom_alignseq(data = dna_columns, mode = "rows", size = 3.5) +
  facet_wrap(vars(track), ncol = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(n = 4)) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_x_grid = FALSE)
```

For larger regions, `mode = "markers"` draws differences and uses `details`
only for selected callouts. Match `track` names to existing annotation
panels when adding DNA detail to a comparison. The [AS3MT example](as3mt-splice-variants-demo.html)
uses this approach at a real locus.

# 9. Equal gene slots for a presence and order comparison

Base-pair spacing can obscure corresponding gene families across loci. A
shared slot template makes occupied and empty positions visible, changing
the meaning of the x axis to comparison slots.

## Present the input

These synthetic clusters have genes assigned to three slots. Cluster B has
no row for slot 2; this input omission alone does not establish gene loss.

```{r workflow-slot-input}
slot_input <- data.frame(
  cluster = c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B"),
  position = c(100, 300, 1000, 500, 900),
  slot = c("s1", "s2", "s3", "s1", "s3"),
  strand = c("+", "-", "+", "-", "+")
)
knitr::kable(slot_input)
```

## Prepare the plotting data

Retain genomic positions in `x`. The strip scale maps these to the explicit
template rather than requiring us to overwrite source coordinates.

```{r workflow-slot-object}
slot_data <- transform(slot_input, x = position, y = 1, track = cluster,
                       gene_key = slot, genomic_x = position)
slot_order <- c("s1", "s2", "s3")
```

## Choose the geom, scales, facet, and theme

`geom_genebox()` uses equal-size squares with strand arrows.
`strip_scale_x()` reserves every slot, including unoccupied ones.
`scale_x_facet_labels()` names each facet's slots, and `coord_fixed()` keeps
boxes square. The clean theme retains ordinary axis labels.

```{r workflow-slots, fig.height = 2.8, fig.alt = "Two three-slot gene clusters. Cluster B has an empty middle slot; occupied slots contain strand arrows."}
ggexon(slot_data) +
  geom_genebox(data = slot_data, aes(fill = slot), box_size = 0.65) +
  facet_grid(. ~ cluster) +
  strip_scale_x(slot_order = slot_order, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_facet_labels(
    cluster, labels = list(A = c("A1", "A2", "A3"), B = c("B1", "B2", "B3"))
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(s1 = "#0072B2", s2 = "#D55E00", s3 = "#009E73")) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1) +
  theme_ggexon_clean(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "none")
```

The x axis now names supplied slots, not base pairs. With Syn-backed data,
`geom_genebox(anchor = "start")`, `"middle"`, or `"end"` chooses the coding
anchor before scaling. See the [Hox example](hox-cluster-expansion-demo.html)
for real annotations, slot curation, and anchor comparisons.

# 10. Align genomic tracks to a tree

A phylogenetic ordering can make a multi-genome comparison easier to read.
ggexon aligns one spanning rectangular tree to genomic rows without manual
positioning of separate plots.

## Present the input

Reuse the synthetic gene intervals from example 5 and supply a synthetic
Newick tree. Its branch lengths are illustrative. This optional example
requires `ape` and `ggtree`.

```{r workflow-tree-input}
tree_text <- "(reference:0.1,query:0.2);"
tree_text
knitr::kable(genes)
```

## Prepare the objects

Tree-tip names must match track IDs, or be mapped with the `individual`
argument to `geom_genomic_tree()`.

```{r workflow-tree-object}
tree_available <- requireNamespace("ape", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("ggtree", quietly = TRUE)
if (tree_available) {
  teaching_tree <- ape::read.tree(text = tree_text)
  tree_tracks <- transform(genes, track = as.character(track))
}
```

## Choose the geom, scales, facet, and theme

`geom_genomic_tree()` attaches the tree; `facet_genomictree()` orders and
aligns the panels. Genomic x ranges and tree branch lengths have separate
scales and meanings. This compact view hides the branch-length ruler;
branch lengths remain specified in the Newick input.

```{r workflow-tree-plot, warning = FALSE, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "A synthetic two-tip tree aligned with reference and query gene tracks."}
if (tree_available) {
  ggexon(tree_tracks) +
    geom_genetag(aes(fill = gene), show_label = FALSE) +
    geom_genomic_tree(tree = teaching_tree, tree_width = grid::unit(1.2, "in")) +
    facet_genomictree(scales = "free_x", show_tree_x_axis = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(A = "#0072B2", B = "#D55E00")) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_number()) +
    theme_ggexon_genomictree(base_size = 10)
} else {
  cat("Install ape and ggtree to render this optional example.")
}
```

For repeated multi-locus comparisons, store comparable windows in a
`SynLocusSet`, attach it with `add_locus_set()`, and use `use_locus_grid()`.
This records the chosen loci alongside the individuals.

# 11. Correct an annotation and compare the result

A gene-model correction is easier to review when it remains attached to the
annotation and you can still plot the original. A patch records the target,
replacement features, and a name for the change.

## Present the correction

Shorten gene A's middle exon from 590 to 560 in this synthetic exercise.
Supply the complete corrected gene model, including its unchanged children.

```{r workflow-patch-input}
corrected_ranges <- query_features(model, genes = "geneA", feature_type = NULL, all = TRUE)
change <- as.character(S4Vectors::mcols(corrected_ranges)$type) %in% c("exon", "CDS") &
  BiocGenerics::start(corrected_ranges) == 501
BiocGenerics::end(corrected_ranges)[change] <- 560L
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(corrected_ranges)[,
  c("start", "end", "type", "gene_id", "transcript_id")])
```

## Construct and apply the patch

```{r workflow-patch-object}
correction <- SynAnnotationPatch(
  name = "shorter-middle-exon", target_ids = "geneA", mode = "replace",
  patch_data = corrected_ranges
)
corrected_model <- patch_annotation(model, correction)
names(list_patches(corrected_model))
```

`patch_annotation_from_gff()` imports corrections from a small GFF. Replacing
models clears stale sequence caches; recompute derived sequences afterwards.

## Choose the geom, scales, facet, and theme

Retain the same base-pair scale before and after to compare the boundary.
Use uncompressed `geom_exon2()` models so the direction arrows sit at the
terminal exons in this compact comparison.

```{r workflow-patch-plot, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Before and after synthetic annotation panels showing a shorter middle exon following a patch."}
before <- load_annotation(SynIndividual(
  annotation_file = gtf_file, annotation_format = "gtf", id = "before"
))
after <- load_annotation(SynIndividual(
  annotation_file = gtf_file, annotation_format = "gtf", id = "after"
))
after <- patch_annotation(after, correction)
curation <- add_individual(SynSpecies("Annotation curation"), before)
curation <- add_individual(curation, after)
ggexon(curation) +
  geom_exon2(aes(fill = transcript_id), chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 980),
             compress_introns = FALSE, arrow_width = 12) +
  facet_genomics(vars(track), ncol = 1, scales = "fixed", strip.position = "left") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = transcript_colours) +
  scale_panel_annotation("fixed_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(100, 500, 900)) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10) +
  theme_ggexon_side_strips("left", base_size = 10)
```

# 12. Query a VCF layer and mark variant positions

A VCF records allele changes at genomic positions. The feature annotation and
variant layer remain separate: attaching a VCF does not change the gene model.
This short example reuses `model` from the first example.

## Present the input

Create three synthetic single-nucleotide variants on the same `chr1` as the
teaching GTF. VCF `POS` uses one-based coordinates; these example alleles are
teaching labels and have not been checked against a reference FASTA.

```{r workflow-vcf-input}
vcf_lines <- c(
  "##fileformat=VCFv4.2",
  "#CHROM\tPOS\tID\tREF\tALT\tQUAL\tFILTER\tINFO",
  "chr1\t125\tv1\tA\tG\t60\tPASS\t.",
  "chr1\t535\tv2\tC\tT\t80\tPASS\t.",
  "chr1\t925\tv3\tG\tA\t50\tPASS\t."
)
cat(vcf_lines, sep = "\n")
vcf_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".vcf")
writeLines(vcf_lines, vcf_file)
```

## Construct and inspect the object

Attach a named `SynVCFAnnotation`, retrieve it, and query the displayed
interval. Plain-text VCF is sufficient for this small example. Large BGZF VCFs
can use a tabix index for regional access. BCF parsing is unavailable.

```{r workflow-vcf-object}
variant_model <- add_annotation(
  model, SynVCFAnnotation(name = "variants", vcf_file = vcf_file)
)
variant_rows <- as.data.frame(query_variants(
  get_annotation(variant_model, "variants"),
  chr = "chr1", start = 80, end = 980
))
knitr::kable(variant_rows[, c("CHROM", "POS", "ID", "REF", "ALT")])
variant_rows$allele <- paste0(variant_rows$REF, ">", variant_rows$ALT)
```

## Choose the geoms, scales, and theme

Use the stored feature annotation for exon models and an ordinary
`geom_vline()` for the queried variant positions. Both use the same genomic
x coordinates. The lines mark sites across transcript rows; they do not
represent frequencies, coverage, or allele-specific transcript structures.

```{r workflow-vcf-plot, fig.height = 3.2, fig.alt = "Three synthetic variant sites marked as vertical lines across two gene A transcript models."}
vcf_plot <- ggexon(variant_model) +
  geom_exon(chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 980), fill = "grey65",
            transcript_arrow_length = 25) +
  geom_vline(
    data = variant_rows, aes(xintercept = POS, colour = allele),
    linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "dashed", inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("A>G" = "#0072B2", "C>T" = "#D55E00", "G>A" = "#009E73"),
                      name = "REF > ALT") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(100, 500, 900), labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_legend = TRUE)
vcf_plot
```

# Choose a view for your question

| Question | Object or preparation | Geometry | Scale and theme |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Which exons and isoforms are annotated? | `SynIndividual` + features | `geom_exon()` | Genomic bp; track theme |
| How do exon structures compare across long introns? | Feature layer | `geom_exon2()` | `scale_x_ggexon_genomic()`; piecewise guide |
| What is the order and direction of genes? | Feature layer + plot labels | `geom_genetag()`, `geom_genelabel()` | Genomic bp or strip scale; track theme |
| Which intervals align between genomes? | `SynSpecies` + `SynPairAlignment` | `geom_nuclink()` | Independent genomic x; pairwise theme |
| Which curated genes or blocks correspond? | Matched interval table | `geom_synteny_link()` | Shared family palette; pairwise theme |
| How does signal vary across a locus? | `SynBigWigAnnotation` | `geom_coverage()` | Genomic x; explicit coverage y policy |
| Where are protein domains and mutations? | Mutation and domain tables/layers | `geom_protein_lollipop()`, `geom_motif()`, `geom_aa_variant()` | Protein residues or projected genomic bp |
| Where are genomic variants recorded? | `SynVCFAnnotation` + `query_variants()` | Exons + ordinary `geom_vline()` | Genomic bp; track theme |
| Which bases differ in an existing alignment? | `alignseq_data()` | `geom_alignseq()` | Anchored genomic coordinates; track theme |
| Which comparison slots are occupied? | Gene-slot table | `geom_genebox()` | `strip_scale_x()`, facet labels; clean theme |
| How do loci relate to a supplied tree? | Matching tracks and tree | `geom_genomic_tree()` | `facet_genomictree()`; genomic-tree theme |

`theme_ggexon_base()` is the common background-free foundation;
`theme_ggexon_clean()` keeps ordinary axes and grids. Choose the track theme
when y only positions annotations; retain a numeric y axis for quantitative
summaries. Side-strip styling supplements a theme and must match the facet's
`strip.position`. Add ordinary `theme()` overrides after the complete theme.

Export a saved plot object with explicit dimensions and inspect the result.
For example, `ggsave("exon-models.pdf", plot = p_exons, width = 9, height = 3.5)`
exports the first model view.

The [Classes, Geoms, Facets, and Guides](ggexon-classes-and-verbs.html)
article provides the full object hierarchy and less common workflows.
The linked biological examples expand these recipes with documented sources.
